system:
You are the reading pass of an illustration engine. You read one large division of a work (a whole text such as a scripture, a novel or a story collection) and return its skeleton as JSON. The engine later draws pictures of the text's moments, so for every stretch of text it needs to know who is on stage and where, and it needs a draft brief for illustrators.

The text comes as numbered units. Each unit line starts with its id (for example `17:4` or `[12]`). Lines starting with `##` are headings, not units.

Return:

1. characters: one entry per individual (a person, a being, or an animal that acts) who appears in or is named in the text.
   - One individual is one entry, even when the text uses different names, titles or descriptions for them. List every form in `aliases`: other names, nicknames, titles, descriptions, and disguises or assumed names.
   - Different individuals who share a name or a title get separate entries, one each. Never fold two people into one entry because they share a name. When a title passes from one holder to another (a ruler dies or is succeeded, an office changes hands), the new holder is a new entry. The `note` must say in one line who this is and how to tell them apart from anyone else with the same name: whose child, spouse or servant they are, their role, and where in the text they appear.
   - A disguised, renamed or unnamed person who the text later identifies is the same entry as their named self, with the disguise or description in `aliases`. If you suspect two entries are one individual but the text does not settle it, keep both and set `same_person_as` on the less certain one to the other's id; otherwise set it to "".
   - Skip people who occur only inside a list of names (a genealogy or roster) and never act.
   - Add a group (an army, a crowd, a household) only when it acts as one on stage, with kind "group".
2. locations: one entry per place where action happens, with aliases and a one-line note. Include places the text refers to only by description ("the sea", "the valley", "the house") when the context shows which place it is, under the place's proper name if the work gives one anywhere.
3. sections: split the text into story sections, runs of consecutive units that tell one episode, the way a study edition's headings or a novel's scenes do. Start a new section when the time, the place or the main action changes. Every unit belongs to exactly one section; sections are in order, with no gaps and no overlaps. A section usually spans 5 to 30 units; prefer fewer, longer sections to many short ones, and never split one continuous scene, conversation or battle. Give the ids of each section's first and last unit and a short title. For each section:
   - setting: ids of the locations where its action happens.
   - on_stage: ids of every character present in the section's action, whether the section names them or only refers to them by a pronoun, a title or a description, or does not mention them but they are clearly there.
   - mentioned_only: ids of characters the section names or refers to who are not present.
4. brief: a draft brief for illustrators, for this division only. It holds only what is true across the whole division or a whole stretch of its world: one person or place is described in the cast, not here, and one episode's look belongs to its section, not here.
   - tone: one line on the mood the pictures should carry.
   - depiction_rules: a short list of how certain things in this text may or may not be shown, drawn from the text and from what you know about the work.
   - era: the stretch of the world this division is set in: a name, its people (who lives there and what they look like), dress, buildings and objects, and technology (what exists and what does not yet exist).
   Keep the brief under 200 words.

Use short, stable snake_case ids (for example `david`, `the_queen`, `main_street`). Section entries may only use ids from your own characters and locations lists. Do not quote the text.

characters.name: Moses
characters.note: Hebrew leader raised in Pharaoh's household, later the deliverer who leads Israel out of Egypt; son of Amram and Jochebed, husband of Zipporah, brother of Aaron; appears throughout Exodus.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.note: Elder brother of Moses, son of Amram and Jochebed; spokesman and later high priest; appears from chapter 4 onward.

characters.name: Yahweh
characters.note: The deity who speaks, acts, and appears in fire, cloud and voice; present across Exodus.

characters.name: Pharaoh
characters.note: The king who did not know Joseph and enslaved Israel, hardens his heart against Moses; unnamed in the text, the Pharaoh of chapters 1 through 14, to be distinguished from later Pharaohs of the same title.

characters.name: Pharaoh's daughter
characters.note: Princess who finds baby Moses in the reeds and adopts him; appears only in chapter 2.

characters.name: Miriam
characters.note: Sister of Moses and Aaron, prophetess who watches over baby Moses and leads the women's song at the sea; appears in 2:4 and 15:20-21.

characters.name: Shiphrah
characters.note: One of two Hebrew midwives who defy Pharaoh's order to kill the boys; appears in chapter 1 only, distinct from Puah.

characters.name: Puah
characters.note: The second Hebrew midwife, with Shiphrah, who fears God and saves the boys; appears in chapter 1 only.

characters.name: Jethro
characters.note: Priest of Midian, father of Zipporah, who gives Moses a home and later counsels him to appoint judges; appears in chapters 2, 3, 4 and 18.

characters.name: Zipporah
aliases: the daughter of the priest of Midian
characters.note: Daughter of Jethro, wife of Moses, who circumcises their son at a lodging place; appears in chapters 2, 4 and 18.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.note: Moses' young attendant who fights Amalek and accompanies him up the mountain; appears in chapters 17, 24, 32 and 33.

characters.name: Amalek
characters.note: Enemy people who attack Israel at Rephidim; appear as a group in chapter 17.

characters.name: Hur
characters.note: Companion of Moses and Aaron who holds up Moses' hands during the battle with Amalek; appears in chapters 17 and 24.

characters.name: Bezalel
characters.note: Craftsman of the tribe of Judah called by Yahweh to build the tabernacle; appears in chapters 31, 35-38.

characters.name: Oholiab
characters.note: Craftsman of the tribe of Dan who works with Bezalel on the tabernacle; appears in chapters 31, 35, 36 and 38.

characters.name: the Egyptians
characters.note: The Egyptian people and their officials, taskmasters and magicians; act as a group in the plague and sea narratives.

characters.name: the children of Israel
characters.note: The Israelite people, who act as a group; present in most chapters.

characters.name: the elders of Israel
characters.note: Israelite elders who are gathered by Moses and Aaron and who go up part way on the mountain; a group.

characters.name: Nadab and Abihu
characters.note: Sons of Aaron who go up the mountain with the elders in chapter 24; named and later mentioned as priests.

characters.name: the taskmasters
aliases: the officers of the children of Israel
characters.note: Egyptian overseers who drive Israel's labor, and the Israelite officers beaten by them; a group.

locations.name: Egypt
locations.note: Land of bondage from which Israel is led out; setting of the plagues and of the Passover.Chapters 1 through 13.  .

locations.name: Goshen
locations.note: Region of Egypt where the Israelites live and where the plagues do not fall; referenced in 8:22, 9:26.

locations.name: Pithom and Raamses
locations.note: Store cities built by Israelite labor for Pharaoh; referenced in chapter 1 and as the starting point of the Exodus in 12:37.

locations.name: the river Nile
locations.note: The river where baby Moses is set adrift and into which Aaron's rod turns the waters to blood.

locations.name: Midian
locations.note: Land where Moses flees and dwells with Jethro; site of the well and the flock.

locations.name: Mount Sinai
locations.note: The mountain where Yahweh appears in the bush and on which the Law is given.

locations.name: the wilderness
locations.note: Desert through which Israel travels from the sea to Sinai and beyond.

locations.name: the Red Sea
locations.note: Sea that is divided so Israel passes on dry ground and then closes over the Egyptian army.

locations.name: the tabernacle and its court
locations.note: The portable sanctuary and courtyard built in the wilderness, where Yahweh dwells among Israel; described in chapters 25-27 and 35-40.

locations.name: Rephidim
locations.note: Camp in the wilderness where Israel lacks water and fights Amalek.

locations.name: the camp
locations.note: The Israelite encampment in the wilderness, which is the setting for the golden calf and the tent outside it.

sections.title: Birth of Moses and his rescue
Return to Egypt and the elders
The rod and the river turned to blood
Death of the firstborn and the Passover
Water from the rock and the battle with Amalek
The Ten Commandments and the altar law

brief.tone: Awe-struck and monumental, with mounting dread in the plague and sea scenes and quiet reverence in the sanctuary chapters.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is not shown in human form; depict only fire, cloud, voice, or light, as the text does.
Show the plagues as natural catastrophes filling the land, not as cartoonish spectacle.
Do not depict the golden calf worship as celebratory; show it as transgression.
Depict the tabernacle and its furnishings as described, drawing on the stated materials, without inventing ornament beyond the text.
Moses should not be shown with horns; the shining face is rendered as light only.

era.name: Bronze Age Egypt and the Sinai wilderness (c. 13th century BCE, traditional setting)
era.people: Egyptians with dark skin and linen-wrapped dress, Hebrew slaves in rough undyed tunics, Midianite herders of the desert, Amalekite warriors.
era.dress: Linen kilts and wigs for Egyptians; coarse wool and linen tunics for Israelites; for priests, fine linen tunics, blue, purple and scarlet woven robes, ephod with gold and onyx; for Pharaoh, royal headdress and jewelry.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick and stone monumental architecture, storage cities, chariots, papyrus baskets and tents of goats' hair; in the wilderness, a portable tabernacle with acacia boards, gold-covered ark, lampstand, bronze altar and linen-hung courtyard.
era.technology: Chariots, bronze and gold metalwork, weaving and dyeing, and writing on stone tablets; no iron tools, no coinage, no mechanized devices, and no glass.
